lead: Where most IT careers start, and the first cert on the 20 year career path. Two exams prove you can build, fix and support the hardware, networks and operating systems every unit runs on.
objSub: A+ is two exams. Switch between Core 1 and Core 2 above; each has its own domains and its own progress. Tick objectives off as you study; your progress stays on this device.
planSub: Set how many hours a week you can give it. The plan covers both exams, about 80 hours each: domains split by exam weight, then a practice stretch before each test.

core1.label: Core 1
core1.note: Mobile devices, networking, hardware, virtualization and cloud, and hardware and network troubleshooting. Most people take Core 1 first, but either order works.
core1.onote: Summary bullets from CompTIA's V15 Core 1 page. The full objectives PDF breaks each domain into numbered sub-objectives.

domains.name: Mobile Devices
obj: Installing components like batteries, cameras and Wi-Fi antennas.
Configuring USB, Bluetooth, NFC and docking stations.
Configuring Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular data and sync settings.
Finding and fixing mobile hardware and connectivity problems.

obj: Networking protocols, ports and wireless technologies.
Setting up small office and home office networks, including IP addressing and VPNs.
Troubleshooting with crimpers, cable testers and Wi-Fi analyzers.

domains.name: Hardware
obj: Setting up RAM, CPUs and storage devices.
Working with HDMI, Ethernet and USB cables.
Installing and maintaining printers, scanners and other peripherals.
Configuring motherboards, power supplies and cooling.

domains.name: Virtualization and Cloud Computing
obj: Virtual machines, hypervisors and desktop virtualization.

domains.name: Hardware and Network Troubleshooting
obj: Identifying and fixing hardware, network and connectivity problems.

core2.label: Core 2
core2.note: Operating systems, security, software troubleshooting and operational procedures. Take both cores from V15; CompTIA doesn't allow mixing versions.
core2.onote: Summary bullets from CompTIA's V15 Core 2 page. The full objectives PDF breaks each domain into numbered sub-objectives.

domains.name: Operating Systems
obj: Working with Windows, macOS, Linux and mobile operating systems.
Managing systems with Task Manager, Command Prompt and Disk Management.
Handling file systems, updates and OS upgrades.

domains.name: Security
obj: Encryption, access controls and wireless security protocols.

domains.name: Software Troubleshooting
obj: Diagnosing and resolving operating system and application problems.
Connectivity, app and performance issues on mobile devices.
Fixing unauthorized access and malware issues.

domains.name: Operational Procedures
obj: Best practices for system changes and documentation.
Following safety protocols and communicating effectively.
Setting up workstation backups and recovery processes.

extras.title: Troubleshooting method
rows: Establish a theory of probable cause (question the obvious).
Test the theory to determine the cause.
Establish a plan of action and implement the solution.
Verify full system functionality and, if applicable, put preventive measures in place.

method: Use the domains above as your checklist, one core at a time. Core 1 first is the usual order.
Pick one video course per core and finish it end to end. Take notes in your own words.
Open up a PC, build a VM, crimp a cable. A+ rewards people who have actually touched the hardware.
Flashcards for ports, connectors, Windows commands and the troubleshooting steps.
Timed practice exams for each core. Review every miss. A common target is 85%+ twice in a row before you book.
tips: They often come first and eat time. Flag them, finish the multiple choice, then come back.
BEST, FIRST and MOST change the answer. Several options can be true; only one fits the qualifier.
Troubleshooting questions follow CompTIA's six steps. Ask which step the scenario is on.
There is no penalty for a wrong answer, so always pick something.

quiz.q: A small office wants a 4-drive array that keeps working if ANY single drive fails, while giving the most usable storage. Which RAID level fits?
o: RAID 5
Right. Striping with parity survives one drive failure and loses only one drive's worth of space (75% usable with 4 drives).
RAID 0
Striping only. Fast, but if any drive dies the whole array is lost.
RAID 1
Mirroring survives a failure, but it's a 2-drive setup and gives only 50% usable space.
RAID 10
Survives a failure, but mirroring costs half the capacity, so it's less storage than RAID 5.

quiz.q: A workstation shows an IP address of 169.254.37.12 and can't reach anything on the network. What is the MOST likely cause?
o: It couldn't reach a DHCP server
Right. 169.254.x.x is APIPA: Windows assigns it to itself when no DHCP server answers.
The DNS server is down
A DNS outage breaks name lookups, but the PC would still have a valid DHCP address.
Another device has the same IP
An IP conflict shows a conflict warning; it doesn't produce a 169.254 address.
The subnet mask was typed wrong
A bad manual mask causes reachability problems, but the address itself wouldn't be 169.254.x.x.

quiz.q: Pages from a laser printer come out with toner that smears or rubs off when touched. Which component should the technician check FIRST?
o: Fuser assembly
Right. The fuser melts toner into the paper. If it isn't hot enough, toner sits loose on the page.
Imaging drum
A damaged drum causes repeating marks or spots at regular intervals, not loose toner.
Transfer roller
A failing transfer roller gives faint or blank pages because toner never reaches the paper.
Toner cartridge
Low toner causes faded prints. The toner that is printed would still be fused properly.

quiz.q: A technician has established a theory of probable cause and confirmed it by testing. According to CompTIA's troubleshooting method, what comes NEXT?
o: Establish a plan of action and implement the solution
Right. Step 4 comes after the theory is confirmed (step 3).
Verify full system functionality
That's step 5, after the fix is in place.
Document findings, actions and outcomes
Documentation is the last step (6).
Question the user and identify changes
That's part of step 1, identifying the problem, which already happened.

quiz.q: A team wants to run several virtual servers directly on bare-metal hardware, with no host operating system underneath, for the best performance. What do they need?
o: A Type 1 hypervisor
Right. Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisors run directly on the hardware, like ESXi or Hyper-V Server.
A Type 2 hypervisor
Type 2 runs as an app on top of a host OS, like VirtualBox on Windows. That adds overhead.
Containers
Containers share the host OS kernel, so they still need an operating system underneath.
Desktop virtualization (VDI)
VDI delivers desktops to users. It runs on top of a hypervisor; it isn't the hypervisor.

quiz.q: A user needs a USB drive that can store a single 6 GB video file and be read AND written on both Windows and macOS without extra software. Which file system?
o: exFAT
Right. No 4 GB file-size limit, and both Windows and macOS read and write it natively.
FAT32
FAT32 is cross-platform but can't hold a file larger than 4 GB.
NTFS
macOS can read NTFS but can't write to it without extra software.
APFS
Apple's file system. Windows can't read it without third-party tools.

quiz.q: A user gets a phone call from someone claiming to be the help desk, asking for the six-digit code from their authenticator app to “fix their account.” What is this?
o: Vishing
Right. Voice phishing: social engineering over the phone, here aimed at stealing an MFA code.
Phishing
Phishing usually means email. The phone channel makes this vishing.
Whaling
Whaling targets senior executives. Nothing here says the user is one.
Shoulder surfing
Shoulder surfing is watching someone's screen or keypad in person.

quiz.q: A technician is setting up a new SOHO wireless router. Which configuration provides the STRONGEST security?
o: WPA3 with SAE
Right. WPA3 uses SAE in place of the pre-shared key handshake, which resists offline password guessing.
WPA2 with TKIP
TKIP is deprecated and weak. Even WPA2 should use AES (CCMP), not TKIP.
WEP with a long key
WEP can be cracked in minutes no matter how long the key is.
WPA2 with WPS enabled
WPS PINs can be brute-forced, which undermines WPA2.

quiz.q: After a Windows update, a laptop is stuck in a reboot loop. The user needs it working today and must keep their files. What should the technician try FIRST?
o: Use Windows Recovery Environment to uninstall the latest update
Right. The update is the most recent change, so roll it back first. It's the least destructive fix and keeps the files.
Reinstall Windows and format the drive
This destroys the user's files, and it's far more than the problem needs.
Reset this PC and choose Remove everything
This also wipes personal files. It's a last resort.
Replace the SSD
Nothing points to hardware failure; the problem started right after a software update.

quiz.q: During a repair, a technician finds what appears to be illegal content on a user's computer. What should the technician do FIRST?
o: Stop, leave the system as is, and report it through the proper channels
Right. Preserve the evidence and follow your organization's policy so chain of custody stays intact.
Delete the content and finish the repair
Deleting destroys evidence and may itself be a crime.
Copy the files to a USB drive to show a supervisor
Copying alters evidence and breaks chain of custody.
Finish the repair, then mention it to the user
Continuing to work on the system can change evidence, and the user may be the subject.

pbqs.title: Match each task to its protocol and port
pbqs.scenario: A small office is setting up its network. For each task, pick the protocol it uses and the port that protocol listens on by default.

rows.req: Manage a Linux server's command line over an encrypted session.
rows.why: SSH on 22. It replaced Telnet (23), which sends everything, passwords included, in clear text.

rows.req: Take over a Windows workstation's desktop remotely.
Turn names like intranet.local into IP addresses.
rows.why: DNS on 53 (UDP for most lookups, TCP for large responses and zone transfers).

rows.req: Hand out IP addresses to devices automatically.
rows.why: DHCP: servers listen on 67, clients on 68. A device that can't reach DHCP falls back to a 169.254.x.x APIPA address.

rows.req: Open a shared folder on a Windows file server.
rows.why: Modern Windows file sharing runs SMB directly over 445.

rows.req: Read email while keeping it stored on the server.
rows.why: IMAP on 143 keeps mail on the server. POP3 (110) downloads it and usually deletes it from the server.

pbqs.title: Put the laser imaging process in order
pbqs.scenario: A user asks why pages come out of the laser printer warm. Walk them through the imaging process by giving each stage its step number.

items.text: Heat and pressure melt the toner into the paper.
items.why: Step 6. It's why pages come out warm, and a weak fuser makes toner smear or rub off.

items.text: The drum gets a uniform negative charge.
items.why: Step 2. The primary charge roller (or corona) preps the drum.

items.text: Leftover toner is wiped off the drum and its charge is removed.
items.why: Step 7. It readies the drum for the next page.

items.text: The printer turns the page data into an image in memory.
items.why: Step 1. The image is built in RAM before anything touches the drum.

items.text: The image moves from the drum onto the paper.
items.why: Step 5. The transfer roller charges the paper so the toner jumps to it.

items.text: A laser writes the image onto the drum by discharging spots.
items.why: Step 3. The laser neutralizes the areas where the image goes.

items.text: Toner sticks to the discharged areas of the drum.
items.why: Step 4. Toner is attracted to the areas the laser exposed.

pbqs.title: Put the malware removal steps in order
pbqs.scenario: A user's laptop shows constant pop-ups and a browser home page that keeps changing back. Put CompTIA's malware removal best practice in order.

items.text: Educate the end user.
items.why: Step 7. Show the user how it likely got in so it doesn't happen again.

items.text: Quarantine the infected system.
items.why: Step 2. Disconnect it from the network so the malware can't spread.

items.text: Enable System Restore and create a restore point.
items.why: Step 6. Only once the system is clean, so the new restore point is clean too.

items.text: Investigate and verify the malware symptoms.
items.why: Step 1. Confirm it's actually malware before acting.

items.text: Remediate: update anti-malware, then scan and remove.
items.why: Step 4. Update definitions first, then scan (safe mode or a boot environment if needed).

items.text: Disable System Restore in Windows.
items.why: Step 3. Old restore points may hold the malware; disabling deletes them.

items.text: Schedule scans and run updates.
items.why: Step 5. Keep the system protected going forward.

pbqs.title: Pick the right Windows tool for each ticket
pbqs.scenario: Six help desk tickets came in this morning. Pick the tool that solves each one. Each answer is used once; two options are distractors.

items.text: A new 2 TB drive shows up in the BIOS but not in File Explorer. Initialize and partition it.
items.why: Disk Management initializes, partitions and formats drives.

items.text: The PC is slow right now. Find the process using 95% CPU and end it.
items.why: Task Manager shows live per-process CPU use and lets you end tasks.

items.text: Windows warns that protected system files may be corrupted. Verify and repair them.
items.why: System File Checker (sfc /scannow) scans and repairs protected system files.

items.text: A laptop blue-screened overnight. Find the error logged right before the crash.
items.why: Event Viewer keeps the System and Application logs, including critical errors before a crash.

items.text: A webcam shows a yellow warning icon after an update. Roll back its driver.
items.why: Device Manager shows device status and has Roll Back Driver in the device's properties.

items.text: A new password policy was pushed, but this PC hasn't picked it up. Apply it now.
items.why: gpupdate /force reapplies all Group Policy settings immediately.

mapSub: A+ starts the 20 year career path and sets up every other one. Tap any cert to jump to it.

keep.text: Renew with 20 continuing education units (CEUs), or by earning a higher CompTIA cert such as Network+ or Security+.
